title: The Curator of Experiments: Gresham College, the Burnt City, and the Law of the Spring
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Curate's Son on the Isle of Wight

stops.name: All Saints', Freshwater, the curate's youngest
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth 18 July 1635 at Freshwater, Isle of Wight, to Cecily Gyles and John Hooke, curate of All Saints' (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). The baptism date of about 26 July is standard in the biographies but was not independently verified here; the church itself is All Saints', Freshwater, per its own Wikipedia article.
stops.campa: John Hooke, curate of All Saints', has his youngest child on the eighteenth of July, and the boy is baptised in his father's own church within the fortnight. The parish sits at the western end of the Isle of Wight, where the chalk downs run out into the sea in stacks and the fields end at a cliff. The child is sickly and not expected to live. His father means him for the church and gives the plan up early, on the grounds of the boy's headaches and the fact that he cannot be kept indoors.
suggested_refs: The parish register of All Saints', Freshwater, for July 1635

stops.name: Freshwater cliffs, the clock taken to pieces
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The childhood material is biographical tradition running back through Waller and Aubrey, not document. The date is a placeholder inside the span c.1638-1648 and carries no evidential weight. The fossil-collecting and the wooden clock are repeated consistently across the biographies; neither is independently attested in a contemporary record reachable here.
stops.campa: The boy is left largely to himself. He walks the foreshore under the chalk gathering fossil shells out of stone that has no business holding shells, and he watches the shipwrights and the millwrights at work in the harbours. He arrives in London a few years later already able to make things, and the traditions that account for it run back through Waller and Aubrey to no document at all: a brass clock taken to pieces, understood, and copied entire in wood; a model ship with rigging and small guns that fire.
sources: Richard Waller, 'The Life of Dr. Robert Hooke' (1705), as relayed in the biographical literature
suggested_refs: The chalk foreshore and fossil beds west of Freshwater Bay

stops.name: Freshwater, forty pounds and a placement in London
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death and the legacy: John Hooke died October 1648 leaving his son forty pounds (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). The Lely placement is [R]: the episode is standard but its address and duration are not documented, and it cannot be pinned to Lely's Covent Garden Piazza house, which he did not occupy until the 1650s or 1660s. Read the London pin as London, not as a street.
stops.campa: John Hooke dies in October and leaves his son forty pounds, which is not a living but is enough to buy a start. The thirteen-year-old is sent up to London and placed with the fashionable portrait painter Peter Lely. He does not stay. The accounts say the smell of the oil paint disagreed with him; they also say he had already seen how the thing was done and did not need to be taught it slowly. Which of those is the reason, or whether either is, the accounts do not settle. He leaves within months with the forty pounds still intact.
suggested_refs: Peter Lely's London studio practice in the late 1640s

stops.name: Westminster School, the headmaster who leaves him room
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hooke was at Westminster under Richard Busby, mastering Latin, Greek, and Euclid (MacTutor). MacTutor gives no exact year inside the span c.1648-1653, and the date here is placed at the start of that span as an ordering device only. The 'six books of Euclid in a week' is admiring biography, not a timed record.
stops.campa: Richard Busby takes him into his own house and teaches him Latin, Greek, some Hebrew and mathematics, and then leaves him alone with an organ and with Euclid. Busby flogged half the bishops of England and is remembered chiefly for the rod; with this pupil he does something else, which is to give a strange boy room. The admiring story is that Hooke went through six books of the Elements in a week. Thirty years on he will design and build a country church for Busby, one of the few of his buildings still standing.
suggested_refs: Busby's headmastership of Westminster School, 1638-1695

segments.name: Oxford: the Engine and the Circle

stops.name: Christ Church, Oxford, the servitor at the organ
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1653 and for the chorister, organist, and servitor arrangement (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). The month is unknown and defaults to January. The irregularity of his standing is itself attested: he did not formally matriculate until 1658.
stops.campa: He goes up to Christ Church as a servitor, paying his way by waiting on wealthier men, singing in the choir, and playing the organ in chapel. It is the bottom rung of the university, and his standing is irregular enough that he does not formally matriculate for another five years. What Oxford gives him is not a degree but an address: within two years he is inside the circle of men who will constitute the Royal Society, brought in to build their apparatus. He is still paying his way by waiting at another man's table.
suggested_refs: The Christ Church buttery and chapel books for the 1650s

stops.name: Wadham College, Wilkins's club and the flying machine
stops.date_confidence: attested that Warden John Wilkins ran an experimental circle at Wadham and that Hooke was drawn into it, meeting Christopher Wren there (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). The flight demonstration to the Oxford Philosophical Club is attested to 1659; it is folded into this stop rather than given a scene of its own, and the 1655 date orders the segment.
stops.campa: John Wilkins, warden of Wadham, keeps an experimental club in his lodgings: Boyle, Wren, Willis, Ward, Petty, and whoever else can be made useful. There is a transparent beehive in the garden and a speaking statue indoors, and the club treats these as continuous with the rest of its business. Hooke is brought in as a pair of hands and stays as a member. In 1659 he lays before the Oxford Philosophical Club a scheme for heavier-than-air flight, builds models worked by artificial muscles, and concludes that no human chest has the power to drive them.
suggested_refs: John Wilkins, Mathematicall Magick (1648), on flight and mechanical devices

stops.name: Beam Hall, Merton Street, Willis's laboratory
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the building. That Hooke assisted Thomas Willis with chemical and anatomical work at Oxford in the later 1650s is standard in the biographical literature; the precise premises are not confirmed by a fetched source. Beam Hall, Merton Street, is Willis's known Oxford house and laboratory, and the coordinate is placed there rather than at the rounded Oxford-centre placeholder the research pool carried.
stops.campa: Thomas Willis keeps his house and his laboratory in Merton Street, and Hooke works there as an assistant at the chemical furnace and at the dissecting table, on terms the record does not preserve. Ten years before the bellows and the dog, he is learning in this room that a body can be taken apart under the eye and its workings shown to another person across a table. Willis is opening skulls and tracing the ring of arteries at the base of the brain. Wren is drawing the plates for him.
suggested_refs: Thomas Willis, Cerebri anatome (1664), with Wren's plates

stops.name: Boyle's laboratory, High Street, the pneumatical engine
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hooke became Boyle's assistant at Oxford and designed the improved air pump used in the vacuum and air-pressure experiments; MacTutor dates the engagement to 1655, the research pool's geography lens to c.1658-1662, and both are in circulation. The date here orders the segment and should not be read as a fixed start. The seven-pounds-a-year figure is standard in the literature and is not carried by the two sources named.
stops.campa: Robert Boyle sets him the problem of Otto von Guericke's vacuum pump, a machine that needs several strong men and does not work well. Hooke redesigns it into a pneumatical engine one operator can work alone: a glass receiver, a rack-and-pinion piston, valves that seal. New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall, printed in 1660 and the ground of what becomes Boyle's law, rests entirely on this machine. John Locke, in the same Oxford circle, follows the results out of it. The engine is Hooke's work and the law carries Boyle's name.
stops.quote: The truth is, the Science of Nature has been already too long made only a work of the Brain and the Fancy: It is now high time that it should return to the plainness and soundness of Observations on material and obvious things.
stops.quote_source: Robert Hooke, Micrographia (London, 1665), Preface, written seven years later
suggested_refs: Robert Boyle, New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall, Touching the Spring of the Air (Oxford, 1660)

stops.name: Christ Church, Oxford, the degrees that arrive late
stops.date_confidence: attested: matriculation 1658, Master of Arts 1662 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). No month is given for the MA and the date defaults to January. Hooke held no university chair at Oxford or Cambridge at any point.
stops.campa: He matriculates in 1658, five years after arriving, and is awarded the Master of Arts in 1662, by which time he is already working in London. The paperwork of his education runs permanently behind the fact of it, and he will never hold a chair at Oxford or Cambridge, nor be offered one. He leaves without patronage, without money, and without a profession. What he leaves with is a reputation among perhaps twenty men for being able to build any instrument that can be described to him in words, and that reputation is what he will live on for the next forty years.
suggested_refs: The Oxford matriculation register, 1658

stops.name: Gresham College, appointed Curator of Experiments
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1662, on Boyle's recommendation, with the obligation to produce demonstration experiments at nearly every weekly meeting (MacTutor). The day is not given and defaults to the first. The Gresham College coordinate is inherited byte-identical from newton.journey.json, edmond_halley.journey.json, john_locke.journey.json, and gottfried_wilhelm_leibniz.journey.json rather than re-derived.
stops.campa: The Society chartered that year needs a man who will produce, at every weekly meeting, three or four experiments demonstrating whatever the Fellows have been arguing about. It is Francis Bacon's Salomon's House put into practice, the imagined college of instruments and trials, and its whole staff is one man. Boyle recommends his assistant. Hooke takes the post in November and holds it for the next forty years, on terms that are exactly what they sound like: the gentlemen debate, and the servant of the house makes the thing happen on the table in front of them.
stops.quote: a sincere Hand, and a faithful Eye, to examine, and to record, the things themselves as they appear
sources: Francis Bacon, New Atlantis (1626), on Salomon's House
suggested_refs: The Royal Society Journal Book, entries for November 1662

stops.name: Gresham College, elected Fellow of the Royal Society
stops.date_confidence: attested, 3 June 1663 (MacTutor). The waiving of his admission fee and weekly subscription on grounds of poverty is standard in the literature and is not carried verbatim by the two sources named here.
stops.campa: On the third of June he is elected a Fellow, and the Society waives his admission fee and his weekly subscription because he cannot pay them. He is now formally a member of the body that formally employs him, and both things stay true for the rest of his life. The Fellows are gentlemen who meet on Wednesdays to watch. He is the man who has spent the week before each meeting building whatever it is they are going to watch. In the minutes for the next forty years he is the curator, not one of the gentlemen.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society's register of Fellows, 3 June 1663

stops.name: Gresham College, the double star and the eye of the fly
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hooke observed and reported the double star Gamma Arietis in 1664 (Wikipedia). No month is given and the date defaults to January. The planetary-rotation observations are attested in the general literature and are not carried by the single source named for the double star.
stops.campa: Turning a telescope on Gamma Arietis in the Ram, he finds it is not one star but two sitting close together, and reports it: the first double star anyone has recorded. He is doing this in his own time, from a college roof, on top of a post that already demands three or four new experiments every week. The minutes take the observation, note it, and go on to the next item of business. Downstairs the same eyes are at the microscope: a flea, a louse, the point of a needle, the mould on a book cover.
stops.quote: The strength and beauty of this small creature, had it no other relation at all to man, would deserve a description.
stops.quote_source: Robert Hooke, Micrographia (London, 1665), Observation LIII, 'Of a Flea'
suggested_refs: Gamma Arietis, the first recorded double star, reported 1664

stops.name: Gresham College, Micrographia
stops.date_confidence: attested: published January 1665 under Royal Society auspices, sixty observations and thirty-eight copperplate engravings, containing the first use of 'cell' for a biological structure (MacTutor; Wikipedia). The Pepys anecdote comes through the British Library's account of the book rather than a fetched reading of Pepys's diary; the wording quoted below is the British Library's report of Pepys, not verified against the diary text itself.
stops.campa: He publishes sixty observations and thirty-eight copperplates drawn from his own eye at the glass: the point of a needle, the edge of a razor, mould, snowflakes, the compound eye of a drone fly, and a flea printed across a folding sheet longer than a man's arm. In a shaving of cork he sees rows of small empty boxes, and calls them cells, because that is what the cells of a monastery look like. Samuel Pepys buys the book, sits up with it until two in the morning, and writes it down as the most ingenious book that ever he read in his life.
stops.quote: these pores, or cells, were not very deep, but consisted of a great many little Boxes, separated out of one continued long pore, by certain Diaphragms
stops.quote_source: Robert Hooke, Micrographia (London, 1665), Observation XVIII, 'Of the Schematisme or Texture of Cork'
sources: British Library, 'Fleas, mould and plant cells under a 17th-century microscope'
suggested_refs: The Royal Society's annotated copy of Micrographia, digitised in full with the plates, 2020

stops.name: Gresham College, the rooms, the salary, and the chair
stops.date_confidence: attested: rooms taken at Gresham in 1664; Curator of Experiments for life 11 January 1665; Gresham Professor of Geometry 20 March 1665 (Wikipedia; MacTutor). The salary is corrected here against a misreading in the research pool: MacTutor gives a Society salary of eighty pounds a year agreed in 1664 with Cutler's fifty-pound mechanical lectureship arranged alongside it, not an eighty-pound package split thirty and fifty.
stops.campa: He moves into rooms at Gresham College on Bishopsgate and never moves out again: bedroom, workshop, laboratory, library, and an observatory on the roof, all in one set of lodgings. The Society agrees eighty pounds a year, and alongside it arranges Sir John Cutler's endowed lectureship in the mechanical arts at fifty, which will go largely unpaid and put him in Chancery for the last decade of his life. In January he is made Curator of Experiments for life. On the twentieth of March he is made Gresham Professor of Geometry, at twenty-nine.
suggested_refs: The Cutlerian lectureship in the mechanical arts, founded at Gresham College 1664

stops.name: Gresham College, the college the fire spared
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Great Fire burned 2-6 September 1666; Gresham College survived and temporarily housed City government and the business of the burnt Royal Exchange (The London Archives, 'Robert Hooke'). That the Royal Society moved to Arundel House as a consequence is attested in newton.journey.json's own correction, which places the Society on the Strand from 1666 to 1673.
stops.campa: The fire burns from the second of September to the sixth and takes four fifths of the walled city, eighty-seven parish churches, and the Royal Exchange. Gresham College, out at the eastern edge, stands. Within days the Lord Mayor, the aldermen, and the merchants of the vanished Exchange are conducting the business of London out of the building Hooke lives in, and the Royal Society, turned out of its own rooms by them, decamps to Arundel House on the Strand. Hooke stays where he is and begins drawing a plan for a new city.
sources: Science Museum (UK), 'The Great Fire of London: how science rebuilt a city'
suggested_refs: Hooke's rebuilding plan for London, presented to the City in September 1666

stops.name: Guildhall, the foundations restaked
stops.date_confidence: attested for the work and the volume: at the peak Hooke was measuring and setting out the foundations of ninety private properties a month (Science Museum). The date is corrected from the research pool: the office of City surveyor was created by the Rebuilding Act that received assent in February 1667, so the appointment belongs to 1667, not 1666. The month here orders the segment. Note also a contested claim: Wikipedia alone says Hooke was appointed Surveyor of the Royal Works in 1670, which MacTutor does not know and which conflicts with Christopher Wren's tenure of that office from 1669; it is not asserted here.
stops.campa: The Rebuilding Act creates the office and the City appoints him one of its surveyors. For the next eleven years he works out of the Guildhall, staking out streets, measuring burnt-out cellars, and issuing certificates that tell two neighbours where the wall between them used to stand. At the peak he is setting out the foundations of ninety private properties a month, and the fees make him rich for the first time in his life. Of the 8,394 foundations in the surviving record he is credited with something near three thousand.
sources: Science Museum (UK), 'The Great Fire of London: how science rebuilt a city'
suggested_refs: The City of London surveyors' certificates and foundation books, 1667-1677

stops.name: The Monument, Fish Street Hill, the column built as a telescope
stops.date_confidence: attested for the design with Wren and for the hollow shaft built as a zenith telescope, defeated by traffic vibration (Science Museum). Construction dates are contradictory in the sources: Wikipedia's Monument article states 1671-1677, the Science Museum gives 1673-1679. The contradiction is recorded, not adjudicated; 1671 is used to order the segment because it is the earlier of the two published spans.
stops.campa: With Wren he raises a fluted Doric column at the foot of Fish Street Hill, its height set to the distance from its own base to the baker's house in Pudding Lane where the fire began. The shaft is hollow, and it is hollow deliberately: it is built as a zenith telescope, a fixed vertical sightline for measuring stellar parallax, with a laboratory in the cellar beneath. Within months the traffic on the hill has shaken the instrument past all usefulness. The column stands anyway, and the hinged lid is still there at the top of the shaft.
sources: Science Museum (UK), 'The Great Fire of London: how science rebuilt a city'
Wikipedia, 'Monument to the Great Fire of London'
suggested_refs: The underground laboratory beneath the Monument, and the hinged lid at its summit

stops.name: Arundel House, the Strand, the Society in exile
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Royal Society sat at Arundel House from 1666 until 1673 and that Leibniz demonstrated his calculating machine there in January and February 1673, being elected Fellow on 9 April (gottfried_wilhelm_leibniz.journey.json; newton.journey.json). Coordinate inherited byte-identical from those files. Hooke's presence at the demonstration is not attested by the sources reached here; that he was the Society's curator throughout the Arundel years is. His own rival arithmetic engine is reported in the general literature and is not carried by a fetched source, so treat that clause as [R].
stops.campa: Turned out of Gresham by the City's homeless government, the Society meets for seven years in the Duke of Norfolk's house on the Strand, and Hooke carries his apparatus across London every week to do there what he did at Bishopsgate. In the winter of 1673 Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz brings his stepped calculating machine into this room and turns the crank for the Fellows, who elect him in April. Hooke, by the accounts, examines the machine closely, and shortly afterwards produces an arithmetic engine of his own.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society Journal Book for January-April 1673, on Leibniz's machine

stops.name: Bethlem Hospital, Moorfields, the palace for the mad
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Moorfields Bethlem was designed by Hooke and built rapidly and at great expense between 1675 and 1676; the gate figures 'Melancholy' and 'Raving Madness' were carved in Portland stone by Caius Gabriel Cibber and survive in the Bethlem Museum of the Mind (Wikipedia, 'Bethlem Royal Hospital'; roberthooke.org.uk). The subsidence and the exact facade length are standard in the literature and not carried by those sources. The Royal College of Physicians building on Warwick Lane is attested to Hooke but undated in the pool; it is folded in here rather than staged separately.
stops.campa: He designs the new Bethlem along the north side of Moorfields: one long facade thrown up in eighteen months for the institution London already calls Bedlam. It is admired as a palace and built like a stage set, and it begins settling almost at once into the soft ground of the old city ditch. Caius Gabriel Cibber carves Raving Madness and Melancholy Madness for the gate piers. The building comes down in 1815 and the two stone figures survive it. In the same decade he is at work on the Royal College of Physicians in Warwick Lane, near St Paul's.
suggested_refs: Cibber's 'Raving Madness' and 'Melancholy Madness', Bethlem Museum of the Mind

stops.name: St Paul's Cathedral, the hanging chain inverted
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hooke consulted with Wren on structural questions for the new St Paul's and stated the catenary principle in an anagram (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). The anagram was printed at the end of A Description of Helioscopes (1676), which fixes the date here; the cathedral's dome was designed later. The division of credit between Wren, Hooke, and other hands is explicitly open in the sources and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: Consulted by Wren on the structure of the new cathedral, Hooke sets down the principle of the arch as a Latin anagram at the end of a book about helioscopes: as hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch. Hang a chain from two points and it falls into the one shape that is purely in tension; turn that shape over in stone and it stands purely in compression. The dome that goes up over London is carried on a hidden brick cone whose profile answers to it. Which man supplied which idea is not recoverable from what survives.
sources: Robert Hooke, A Description of Helioscopes (London, 1676)
suggested_refs: The catenary anagram in A Description of Helioscopes (1676), decoded in Waller's Posthumous Works (1705)

stops.name: Gresham College, the dog and the bellows
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1667 by the published account in the Philosophical Transactions, reached here through the research trail rather than by direct fetch of the journal, so confidence is a step below the Wikipedia and MacTutor items in this file. The month is unknown and defaults to January; the demonstration to the Society is often dated to October 1667 in the literature, which was not verified here.
stops.campa: He opens a dog's thorax, cuts away the ribs and the diaphragm, and keeps the animal alive for more than an hour by driving air down a tube into its lungs with a pair of bellows while the chest lies open and motionless. The lungs do not move. The dog does not die. What sustains life is fresh air reaching the blood, not the mechanical action of breathing. He writes afterwards that the suffering of the creature left him unwilling ever to repeat the operation, and he does not repeat it.
sources: Philosophical Transactions, 1667, Hooke's account of the ventilated dog (via research trail, not fetched directly)
suggested_refs: Hooke's 1667 paper on respiration in the Philosophical Transactions

stops.name: Gresham College, hunting the parallax of Gamma Draconis
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hooke mounted a telescope in his own rooms to hunt annual stellar parallax in Gamma Draconis in the span 1669-1674 and that the result did not hold (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). The quotation below is corrected against the primary text: the widely repeated form 'the true understanding of this principle' is the Dictionary of National Biography's adaptation; Hooke's own sentence reads 'thereof', verified in two OCR scans of Lectiones Cutlerianae (1679), which reprints the 1674 pamphlet.
stops.campa: He cuts a hole through the roof and the floors of his own lodgings and mounts a thirty-six-foot telescope vertically through the building to catch Gamma Draconis as it passes overhead, hunting the annual shift that would prove the Earth moves. He publishes four observations and states that he has found it. He has not: the instrument cannot hold the precision the measurement demands, and Bradley will settle the question sixty years later with a better one. The telescope stays mounted where he put it, through the floors of the rooms he lives in.
stops.quote: But this I durst promise the Undertaker, that he will find all the great Motions of the World to be influenced by this Principle, and that the true understanding thereof will be the true perfection of Astronomy.
stops.quote_source: Robert Hooke, An Attempt to Prove the Motion of the Earth from Observations (London, 1674), p. 28, reprinted in Lectiones Cutlerianae (1679)
sources: Robert Hooke, An Attempt to Prove the Motion of the Earth (1674), verified in two OCR scans of Lectiones Cutlerianae (1679)
suggested_refs: James Bradley's 1728 discovery of aberration, made in the course of the same parallax hunt

stops.name: Gresham College, the answer to Newton's light
stops.date_confidence: attested. Newton's letter of 6 February 1672 was read to the Society on 8 February and printed on 19 February; Hooke, as curator, was asked for his judgement and delivered it within the week (newton.journey.json, which corrects the venue to Arundel House for the reading itself). The pin here is Hooke's own Gresham lodging, where he wrote; the reading took place on the Strand.
stops.campa: Newton's paper on colours is read to the Society, and Hooke, as curator, is asked for his opinion on it. He gives it inside a week and at length: the experiments are good and he has done most of them himself, but the conclusion that white light is a mixture does not follow from them, and a good deal of the rest stands already in Micrographia. It is the last civil exchange the two of them have. Newton answers at enormous length, and then for years publishes nothing at all.
sources: newton.journey.json (Arundel House, elected and the light divided)
suggested_refs: Hooke's critique of Newton's 1672 letter on light and colours, Royal Society Letter Book

stops.name: Gresham College, the balance spring claimed
stops.date_confidence: attested that Huygens developed the spiral balance spring in Paris with the clockmaker Isaac Thuret in 1675 and moved to patent it, and that Hooke declared the invention his own, having described a spring-controlled balance to the Society years earlier without printing it (christiaan_huygens.journey.json; Wikipedia). Hooke's claim to have conceived it as early as 1658 is his own assertion, not an independent attestation; the Tompion watch inscribed 'R. Hooke invenit 1658' is reported in the Huygens file.
stops.campa: Christiaan Huygens sends the Society a spring-regulated balance for a watch and moves to patent the design in Paris. Hooke, in the room when the letter is read out, says the invention is his: that he described a spring-controlled balance to these same Fellows years ago, showed them a working watch, and withheld the details only because the Society would not guarantee him terms. Neither man ever gives the claim up. He has Thomas Tompion make him a watch and put on it, in letters anyone can read, R. Hooke invenit 1658.
suggested_refs: The Tompion watch inscribed 'R. Hooke invenit 1658', and Huygens's 1675 Paris patent

stops.name: Gresham College, ceiiinosssttuu decoded
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected against the primary text, verified in two OCR scans of Lectiones Cutlerianae (1679). The anagram was first printed as ceiiinosssttuu, with a double u, at the end of A Description of Helioscopes (1676); it was decoded in De Potentia Restitutiva, or of Spring (1678). Lectiones Cutlerianae (1679) is the collected volume reprinting both, not the place of first appearance, and the modern form 'ceiiinosssttuv' is a normalisation of seventeenth-century u and v. A second, different Hooke anagram, cediinnoopssttuu for 'Ut pondus sic tensio', stands a few pages later and is not the same thing.
stops.campa: Two years after printing an anagram at the end of A Description of Helioscopes, he decodes it: ut tensio, sic vis, as the extension, so the force. Springs, watch balances, loaded beams, and the air itself obey one rule, that the power of a spring stands in the same proportion as the tension of it. It is the law that will carry his name into every physics textbook afterwards, and he had kept it two years in cipher, holding the priority while he worked out what it was worth.
stops.quote: About two years since I printed this Theory in an Anagram at the end of my Book of the Descriptions of Helioscopes, viz. ceiiinosssttuu, id est, Ut tensio sic vis; That is, The Power of any Spring is in the same proportion with the Tension thereof.
stops.quote_source: Robert Hooke, 'De Potentia Restitutiva, or of Spring' (1678), in Lectiones Cutlerianae (London, 1679)
sources: Robert Hooke, De Potentia Restitutiva (1678), verified in two OCR scans of Lectiones Cutlerianae (1679)
Dictionary of National Biography (1885-1900), vol. 27, p. 291
suggested_refs: A Description of Helioscopes (1676), where the anagram is first printed

stops.name: Gresham College, the quarrel with Hevelius
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Society sent Halley, aged twenty-two, to Danzig in 1679 to adjudicate the dispute Hooke had provoked over whether naked-eye sights could match telescopic ones, and that Halley's on-site verdict went against Hooke (edmond_halley.journey.json). The stop sits at Hooke's own pin because the argument is his and the journey to Danzig is Halley's; the month defaults to January.
stops.campa: Johannes Hevelius of Danzig measures star positions with open sights and no telescope, and does it superbly. Hooke argues in print that this cannot be so, that telescopic sights of his own design must beat the naked eye by a wide margin, and the dispute grows personal enough that the Society sends the twenty-two-year-old Edmond Halley to Danzig to settle it in person. Halley observes beside the old man for two months and reports that Hevelius's measurements are as good as he claims them to be.
suggested_refs: Halley's Danzig observations of 1679, made alongside Hevelius

stops.name: Gresham College, the toothed wheel and the flour
stops.date_confidence: attested: the flour-dusted vibrating plate is dated 8 July 1680 and the toothed-wheel pitch demonstration to 1681 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). The two experiments are combined here at the earlier of the two dates. Chladni's figures are named for a later worker; the priority is not in dispute, only the naming.
stops.campa: He spins brass wheels with counted teeth against a card at known rates and shows the Society that musical pitch is nothing but the frequency of the strokes, a note being a number of blows in a second. Then he dusts a glass plate with flour, draws a bow along its edge, and watches the flour walk off the moving parts of the plate and settle into still lines along the nodes. He writes down what the flour does. A century later Chladni will make the same figures famous and give them his own name.
suggested_refs: Ernst Chladni, Entdeckungen über die Theorie des Klanges (1787), on the same nodal patterns

stops.name: Gresham College, the lecture on memory
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hooke delivered a Royal Society lecture in 1682 proposing a mechanical model of memory covering encoding, association, retrieval, and forgetting (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). The month is unknown and defaults to January. The details of the model given here follow the standard summary of that lecture; the lecture text itself, printed by Waller in 1705, was not fetched directly.
stops.campa: He reads the Society a lecture proposing that memory is an organ and a mechanism. Impressions are laid down in a physical chain in the order they arrive; the soul attends to them at a fixed rate; repetition strengthens a chain and disuse lets it decay; recollection is a tracing back along the chain to the place where the thing sits. The lecture stays in manuscript until Waller prints it after his death, and few enough read it then. He works out, in numbers, how many ideas a long life can hold.
sources: Richard Waller, The Posthumous Works of Robert Hooke (London, 1705)
suggested_refs: Hooke's 1682 lecture on memory, printed in Waller's Posthumous Works (1705)

segments.name: The Coffeehouses and the Country Commissions

stops.name: Garraway's Coffee House, Exchange Alley
stops.date_confidence: attested that Hooke's memorandum book records constant traffic through Garraway's and Jonathan's in Exchange Alley, and that the surviving principal diary runs 10 March 1672 to 16 May 1683; the City of London purchased the diary and papers in 1891 and it now holds UNESCO Memory of the World status (The London Archives). The date here sits inside the diary years and orders the segment. The archive reference number carried by the research pool was not re-verified against the archive's own catalogue.
stops.campa: The diary he keeps from 1672 records the other half of the working life: Garraway's in Exchange Alley, and Jonathan's a few doors along, where he meets Wren and Aubrey and Hoskins, argues with instrument makers, lends money at interest, buys books, drinks coffee and chocolate. He notes what he ate, what he took for his stomach, whom he slept with, and how he slept, in a cramped hand with private symbols for the states of his own body. The City bought the volume in 1891 and it is in the London Archives.
sources: Robinson and Adams, eds., The Diary of Robert Hooke 1672-1680 (1935)
suggested_refs: Hooke's memorandum book, 10 March 1672 to 16 May 1683, The London Archives

stops.name: Ragley Hall, Warwickshire, the country practice
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Hooke is credited with work on Ragley Hall for the Earl of Conway around 1679-1680 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'), but the country-house attributions rest on scattered payments and diary notices rather than signed drawings. The coordinate is corrected: the research pool's 52.1922, -1.8106 lands about six kilometres east of the estate, in open country beyond Alcester; Wikipedia's Ragley Hall article gives 52.19795, -1.89611.
stops.campa: Edward Conway sets him to work on a great house in Warwickshire. The country practice runs alongside the City surveying for a decade and leaves a far poorer paper trail than the London commissions: a payment in an account book, a line in the diary, a house afterwards refaced by other hands. He is riding a hundred miles for this work while still owing the Royal Society an experiment every week it meets. How much of the Ragley Hall now standing is his cannot be established from what survives.
suggested_refs: Hooke's diary and account entries for the Conway commission, 1679-1680

stops.name: Willen, the church built for Busby
stops.date_confidence: attested: Hooke designed the brick parish church of St Mary Magdalene at Willen in 1680 for Dr Richard Busby, his own former Westminster headmaster, who endowed it, and it is one of the few Hooke buildings surviving largely as built (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). The coordinate is corrected from the research pool's 52.0453, -0.728, which lands about two kilometres off near Willen Lake; the church's own article gives 52.06234, -0.72015.
stops.campa: Richard Busby, still headmaster at Westminster more than thirty years after beating Latin into him, endows a new brick parish church in a Buckinghamshire village and gives the commission to his old pupil. Hooke builds a plain rectangular box with a west tower, round-headed windows, and no aisles, the classical vocabulary held at its quietest. Of everything he designed in London, the great facades and the hospital and the college and the halls, almost nothing stands. St Mary Magdalene at Willen stands, largely as he built it.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Church of St Mary Magdalene, Willen'
suggested_refs: St Mary Magdalene, Willen, Milton Keynes, built 1680

stops.name: Aske's Hospital, Hoxton, the almshouse from a will
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected. The research pool dated the commission 1679-1690s, which is impossible: Robert Aske died in 1689 and the Hoxton almshouses and school were funded by his will, built on twenty-one acres to Hooke's design by 1692, and demolished in 1824 (Wikipedia, 'Robert Aske (merchant)'). The date here is set at c.1690-1692 and defaults to January 1691. The Hoxton coordinate is an area pin, not a building footprint.
stops.campa: Robert Aske, a Haberdashers' Company merchant, dies in 1689 and leaves money in his will for an almshouse and a school. The Company builds it at Hoxton on twenty-one acres to Hooke's design, a long colonnaded range, and it is standing by 1692. He is in his late fifties, suing a dead man's executors in Chancery for money he was promised at twenty-nine, and still taking commissions from City companies who want a building put up quickly and cheaply and know he can do it. The place is pulled down in 1824.
suggested_refs: The Haberdashers' Company records of Aske's Hospital, Hoxton, 1690-1692

segments.name: The Secretary and the Priority Wars

stops.name: Gresham College, the secretaryship after Oldenburg
stops.date_confidence: attested, with a decade-scale correction. Wikipedia prints 'On 13 September 1667' for the acting secretaryship, which cannot stand: Henry Oldenburg held the office until his death on 5 September 1677. The date is 13 September 1677, eight days after Oldenburg died, which is also what makes the joint secretaryship of 19 December 1677 follow coherently. Do not reproduce the 1667 typo. The lapse of the Philosophical Transactions and the seven numbers of Hooke's Philosophical Collections are standard in the literature and not carried by the sources named.
stops.campa: Henry Oldenburg dies on the fifth of September, having run the Society's foreign correspondence and the Philosophical Transactions since the beginning, and having quarrelled bitterly with Hooke over the balance spring. Eight days later Hooke is acting Secretary; in December he is made joint Secretary with Nehemiah Grew. He now controls what the Society hears from abroad and what it prints. The Transactions lapse under his hand; in their place he brings out seven numbers of his own Philosophical Collections between 1679 and 1682, and then no more.
suggested_refs: Hooke's Philosophical Collections, numbers 1-7 (1679-1682)

stops.name: Newport, Isle of Wight, the brother dead
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Hooke's brother John, a grocer at Newport in business and legal difficulty, died in 1678 in what the record treats as an apparent suicide or fatal self-harm; the research pool itself notes that reconstructions of the death differ between accounts. The month is unknown and defaults to January. That Grace passed into Robert's London household is attested; the sequence relative to the death is not precisely fixed, since she had lived with him from about age ten.
stops.campa: John Hooke the younger, grocer of Newport, in trouble with his creditors and with the law, dies in his own town on the Isle of Wight in what the record treats as a suicide. Robert comes down for the business of it, back to the island for the first time in thirty years. His brother's daughter Grace, who has been in his London household since she was about ten, is now wholly his charge. How the death actually happened is reported differently in different accounts and cannot be settled from them.
suggested_refs: The Newport, Isle of Wight, parish and borough records for 1678

stops.name: Gresham College, the letters to Cambridge
stops.date_confidence: attested: writing as Royal Society secretary, Hooke proposed to Newton in November 1679 that planetary motion be understood as inertial tangential motion compounded with a central attraction, and on 6 January 1680 wrote that gravitational attraction varies in duplicate proportion inversely with distance (Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke'). The two letters are folded into one stop at the later, precisely dated one. That this correspondence restarted Newton's work on orbits is recorded in newton.journey.json.
stops.campa: Writing as Secretary, he opens a correspondence with Newton in November on the composition of orbital motion: not a balance of forces but a straight-line motion continually bent by an attraction toward a centre. He has the idea and puts it in a letter to Cambridge, without the mathematics that would get an ellipse out of it, and he never acquires that mathematics. In January he states the supposition plainly: the attraction between two bodies falls off in duplicate proportion to the distance, inversely as the square.
sources: newton.journey.json (Trinity College, the letter to Hooke)
suggested_refs: The Hooke-Newton correspondence of November 1679 to January 1680, Royal Society Letter Book

stops.name: Gresham College, forty shillings for a proof
stops.date_confidence: attested to 24 January 1684 in edmond_halley.journey.json, which dates the exchange in which Halley presented his derivation from Kepler's third law, Hooke claimed to hold the proof already and would not show it, and Wren offered a prize to whoever produced one. The forty-shilling figure and the book-worth framing follow that file. Halley's ride to Cambridge in August 1684 is recorded in newton.journey.json.
stops.campa: Hooke, Wren, and Halley fall into the question after a meeting: what curve does an inverse-square force produce? Halley has got as far as the inverse-square itself from Kepler's third law and cannot go further. Hooke says he has demonstrated the curve and will not show the demonstration until others have tried and failed, so that they will value it when it comes. Wren, unconvinced, offers a book worth forty shillings to whichever of them produces a proof inside two months. Nobody does. In August Halley rides to Cambridge and asks Newton.
sources: edmond_halley.journey.json (Gresham College, Kepler's third law stop)
suggested_refs: De Moivre's memorandum of Halley's August 1684 visit to Newton, Keynes MS 130

stops.name: Gresham College, Book I laid before the Society
stops.date_confidence: attested, 28 April 1686, in the Royal Society Council minutes; the coordinate and date are inherited byte-identical from newton.journey.json. Newton's published scholium acknowledged Wren, Hooke, and Halley in connection with the inverse-square relation while maintaining that Hooke had supplied no demonstration. Newton's private wording about mathematicians and drudgery is standard in the priority-dispute literature and was not fetched here.
stops.campa: The manuscript of De motu corporum is laid before the Society, and Hooke rises to say that the inverse-square law was his, communicated to Newton in his own letters, and asks for acknowledgement in the printed book. Newton, told of it, threatens to suppress the third book entirely, and Halley talks him down over fifteen months while paying for the printing out of a clerk's salary. The scholium that appears in the printed book names Wren, Hooke, and Halley together, and grants Hooke no demonstration.
sources: newton.journey.json (Gresham College, Book I laid before the Society)
suggested_refs: The scholium to Proposition IV, Book I, of the Principia (1687)

stops.name: Gresham College, Grace
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1687 and corrected. The research pool left the death year open between 1687 and 1689; it should not stay open. Two independent fetched sources give 1687: Wikipedia ('he was devastated when she died in 1687') and Westminster Abbey's commemorations page ('his niece Grace (died 1687)'). The 1689 variant traces only to the enthusiast site roberthooke.org.uk. The month is unknown and defaults to January. Waller's phrase is tagged [R]: it is quoted consistently across the modern biographies but was not confirmed against the 1705 text, whose Wellcome scan is image-only.
stops.campa: Grace Hooke, who came into his house as a child of about ten and kept it for him afterwards, dies. His diary, in its coded symbols, records a sexual relationship with her beginning when she was about sixteen. Her own account of it does not exist and never did. Waller, who knew him, dates the change in him from this death: he was afterwards a different man in the room, and men who had worked beside him for twenty years noticed it. He lives sixteen more years and publishes almost nothing.
stops.quote: less active, more Melancholly and Cynical
stops.quote_source: Richard Waller, 'The Life of Dr. Robert Hooke' (1705), as quoted across the modern biographies; not verified against the 1705 text
sources: Richard Waller, The Posthumous Works of Robert Hooke (1705)
suggested_refs: The coded passages of Hooke's memorandum book concerning Grace Hooke

segments.name: The Last Years and the Missing Face

stops.name: Lambeth Palace, the doctorate that was not Oxford's
stops.date_confidence: corrected, and the correction matters. The research pool had Oxford conferring an honorary MD in 1691, but the word 1691 appears nowhere in the Wikipedia article in connection with a degree, whose only relevant line is the bare footnote that the MD was an honorary degree conferred by Oxford. The standard record, in Waller's Life and the ODNB, is a Lambeth degree of Doctor of Physic granted by Archbishop John Tillotson, in London, in December 1691. MacTutor and roberthooke.org.uk mention no doctorate at all. The day is unknown and defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Archbishop John Tillotson creates him Doctor of Physic by Lambeth degree in December, an archiepiscopal grant rather than a university one. He is fifty-six, has never practised medicine on another person, and has spent thirty years dosing himself with sal ammoniac, iron filings, laudanum, and purges, recording each dose in the diary against the state of his sleep and his bowels. The degree is still commonly reported as an Oxford doctorate. It was not Oxford's.
sources: Richard Waller, 'The Life of Dr. Robert Hooke' (1705), via the ODNB record
Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke' (footnote on the honorary MD)
suggested_refs: The Lambeth degree registers of Archbishop John Tillotson, 1691

stops.name: Westminster Hall, the suit against Cutler's estate
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the precise dates. That Hooke litigated over unpaid Cutlerian lecture income and that the outcome went substantially his way is corroborated in the general chronology; the 1693 date for Sir John Cutler's death and the 1696 Chancery decree come from the research trail and were not re-verified against a primary Chancery record. Treat both years as a step below the directly fetched items in this file. The month is unknown and defaults to January.
stops.campa: Sir John Cutler dies in 1693 having paid, across nearly thirty years, almost none of the fifty pounds a year he endowed for the mechanical lectures Hooke went on delivering anyway. Hooke sues the executors in Chancery. The suit runs for years and a decree in 1696 goes substantially his way, with the arrears. He is by then an old man collecting money he was promised at twenty-nine. He does not spend it. It goes into the iron chest in his rooms at Gresham with the rest of it.
suggested_refs: The Chancery decree of 1696 in Hooke v. Cutler's executors

stops.name: Gresham College, death in his own rooms
stops.date_confidence: attested, 3 March 1703, in his rooms at Gresham College, after a final year reported as blind and bedridden; no autopsy-derived cause of death survives (Wikipedia; Westminster Abbey commemorations page). The chest of about eight thousand pounds in money and gold, the library of over three thousand books, the absence of a will, and the passing of the estate to his cousin Elizabeth Stephens are all attested (Wikipedia).
stops.campa: In his last year he is blind or nearly blind, his legs swollen, and he does not leave his bed. He dies in the rooms at Gresham College he took thirty-nine years earlier, intestate, at sixty-seven, and no cause of death is recorded anywhere. His executors open an iron chest in the lodging and find some eight thousand pounds in coin and gold, untouched, and a library running past three thousand volumes. The estate passes to a cousin, Elizabeth Stephens.
stops.quote: I have obtained my end, if these my small Labours shall be thought fit to take up some place in the large stock of natural Observations, which so many hands are busie in providing.
suggested_refs: The inventory of Hooke's Gresham College rooms taken after his death, March 1703

stops.name: St Helen's, Bishopsgate, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1703 for the burial at St Helen's, Bishopsgate (Wikipedia; Westminster Abbey). The exact day is not given in the sources reached and the sixth is an ordering placeholder, not a record. Waller's Posthumous Works is attested for 1705, printed by Sam. Smith and Benj. Walford for the Royal Society, roughly 505 pages plus fifteen leaves of plates, dedicated to Sir Isaac Newton (Wellcome Collection catalogue record).
stops.campa: He is carried the short distance from Gresham College to St Helen's, Bishopsgate, and buried there in March. No monument was raised that anyone recorded, no inscription survives, and the parish left no note of where in the ground he was laid. Two years later Richard Waller prints The Posthumous Works of Robert Hooke, five hundred pages of folio with a life of the author at the front and fifteen leaves of plates, and dedicates the whole of it to Sir Isaac Newton.
sources: Wellcome Collection, catalogue record for The Posthumous Works of Robert Hooke (1705)
suggested_refs: Richard Waller, The Posthumous Works of Robert Hooke (London, 1705), dedicated to Newton

stops.name: City of London Cemetery, the bones moved east
stops.date_confidence: attested as an assumption and no further. The Westminster Abbey commemorations page states that Hooke's grave was disturbed by nineteenth-century churchyard clearance and that his remains are assumed to lie in a communal reburial at the City of London Cemetery; the word assumed is the Abbey's own and is the operative word. St Helen's own article describes the 1891 remains as translated to Ilford Cemetery, a naming variant for the same ground. The coordinate is corrected from the research pool's 51.5729, 0.0338, which lands on Wanstead Flats; Wikipedia gives 51.56, 0.048 for the cemetery. The date is the 1891 clearance and defaults to January. The research pool also carried a claim that a Hooke memorial stained-glass window at St Helen's was destroyed in the 1993 Bishopsgate bombing; the bombing and the damage to the church are attested, the memorial window specifically is not, and the campa says only what is confirmed.
stops.campa: In the nineteenth century the churchyard at St Helen's is cleared, as London's churchyards are cleared to make room, and the bones taken out of it are carried east and reburied together in common ground outside the city. Hooke is assumed to be among them. Westminster Abbey's own account of him uses exactly that word and goes no further with it. There is no grave, no coffin plate, no marker, and no identification of any kind. The church he was buried in is itself half rebuilt, having been wrecked by the Bishopsgate bomb of 1993 and repaired afterwards.
sources: Wikipedia, 'City of London Cemetery and Crematorium'
suggested_refs: The 1891 clearance of the St Helen's Bishopsgate churchyard and the translation of remains

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the stone in the lantern
stops.date_confidence: attested: a memorial stone to Hooke was unveiled at Westminster Abbey on 3 March 2005, the tercentenary of his death, placed in the lantern area near the grave of Richard Busby, his former Westminster School headmaster (Westminster Abbey commemorations page). The Abbey page gives no inscription text and makes no claim to hold any remains.
stops.campa: Three hundred years to the day after he died, a memorial stone cut with his name is set into the floor of the Abbey, in the lantern, close to the grave of Richard Busby, who taught him Greek and Euclid at Westminster and later gave him the church at Willen to build. Elsewhere in the same building the men he worked beside and quarrelled with, Newton among them, lie under monuments with their faces carved. The Abbey holds no bones of Hooke's and makes no claim to any.
suggested_refs: The Hooke memorial stone, Westminster Abbey lantern, unveiled 3 March 2005

stops.name: Royal Society, Carlton House Terrace, the portrait nobody can find
stops.date_confidence: attested. Felicity Henderson, examining the legend that Newton destroyed a portrait of Hooke, found no order, no eyewitness, and no destruction record implicating Newton, and found the existence of any authentic life portrait doubtful, resting on an ambiguous 1674 diary mention and a 1710 sighting by Zacharias Conrad von Uffenbach that may have misidentified a portrait of Theodore Haak (Royal Society blog, December 2010). MacTutor separately reports that a 'possible portrait' identified at the Society has since been shown to depict someone else. The rival modern candidate identifications, a Mary Beale sitter proposed by Lawrence Griffing and contested as Isaac Barrow, and an earlier candidate reidentified as Jan Baptist van Helmont, are recorded in the research pool as unconfirmed and are not asserted here. The quotation below is corrected: the words are verbatim in the DNB, vol. 27, p. 292, but the DNB silently condensed Waller's opening clause and dropped a parenthesis, so it must be cited as the DNB condensing Waller, not as Waller verbatim.
stops.campa: The story that Newton, taking the presidency the year Hooke died, destroyed his rival's portrait has been repeated for a century. The Society's own historian went looking for it and found no order, no witness, and no record of a destruction, and no good evidence that a portrait from life ever existed at all: one ambiguous line in the diary, and a German traveller's sighting in 1710 that probably describes a picture of somebody else. Every published likeness of Hooke is a modern reconstruction worked up from one paragraph of description, and that paragraph turns out to be the Dictionary of National Biography condensing Waller.
stops.quote: in person but despicable, being crooked and low of stature, and as he grew older more and more deformed. He was always very pale and lean, and latterly nothing but skin and bone, with a meagre aspect, his eyes grey and full, with a sharp, ingenious look whilst younger. He wore his own hair of a dark brown colour, very long, and hanging neglected over his face uncut and lank, which about three years before his death he cut off, and wore a periwig. He went stooping and very fast, having but a light body to carry, and a great deal of spirits and activity, especially in his youth.
stops.quote_source: Dictionary of National Biography (1885-1900), vol. 27, p. 292, condensing Richard Waller, 'The Life of Dr. Robert Hooke', in The Posthumous Works of Robert Hooke (London, 1705)
sources: Royal Society blog, Felicity Henderson, 'Hooke, Newton and the missing portrait' (December 2010)
Dictionary of National Biography (1885-1900), vol. 27, pp. 291-292
Robyn Adams and Lisa Jardine, 'Report: The Return of the Hooke Folio', Notes and Records of the Royal Society 60 (2006), pp. 235-239
suggested_refs: The Hooke Folio, rediscovered and acquired by the Royal Society in 2006, edited online by Lisa Jardine, 2007
